name: Question 2
problem:
Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The $2$nd cosine coefficient of the series is

$$
{a}_{2}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ and $L=3,$ the $2$nd cosine coefficient becomes

$$
{a}_{2}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$
worked_solution:
Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

Therefore, $2$nd cosine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=3$ and $f(x)=F(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {\int }_{-3}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by k≠0 represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of 1k.

Now, let s=πLx. Then, since f(x) has a period of 2L, the function g(s)=f(Lπs) must have a period of 2L⋅πL=2π.

The Fourier series of g(s) is g(s)∼a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(ns)+bnsin⁡(ns), where: a0=1π∫−ππg(s)dsan=1π∫−ππg(s)cos⁡(ns)ds,n≥1bn=1π∫−ππg(s)sin⁡(ns)ds,n≥1

Substituting s=πLx and using the fact that g(s)=f(Lπs), we get the Fourier series of f(x): f(x)∼a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπLx)+bnsin⁡(nπLx)

Therefore, 2nd cosine coefficient of f(x) is a2=1π∫−ππg(s)cos⁡(2s)ds=1π∫−ππf(Lπs)cos⁡(2s)ds=1π∫−LLf(Lπ⋅πLx)cos⁡(2⋅πLx)d(πLx)=1π⋅πL∫−LLf(x)cos⁡(2πLx)dx=1L∫−LLf(x)cos⁡(2πLx)dx.

Finally, substituting L=3 and f(x)=F(x)=ln⁡(x2+1), we get a2=13⋅∫−33ln⁡(x2+1)cos⁡(2π3x)dx.
